opus-5.5.text:
Well, it wasn't really a decision against Meta. It was more that the type of research I've been advocating for, for the better part of a decade, reached a point where it made sense to pursue it in a structure built entirely around it.

I've been saying for years that large language models, as useful as they are, are not the path to human-level intelligence. They're trained on text, and text is a very low-bandwidth, very impoverished representation of the world. A four-year-old child has seen, through vision alone, about as much data as the biggest LLMs are trained on, and that child understands that if you push a glass off a table it falls and breaks. LLMs don't really understand that. They can produce text that sounds like they do, but they don't have a model of the physical world. They can't plan, they don't have persistent memory in a meaningful sense, and they don't really reason. They manipulate language fluently, and we're easily fooled into thinking fluency means intelligence.

So the agenda I've been pushing is what I call objective-driven AI, built around world models. Systems that learn, mostly from video and sensory data, how the world works, in an abstract representation space, not by predicting every pixel. That's the idea behind JEPA, joint embedding predictive architectures. Once you have a world model, you can predict the consequences of your actions, and then you can plan a sequence of actions to achieve a goal, subject to guardrails. That's how you get systems that are both more capable and controllable by design.

At Meta, FAIR did a lot of great work in that direction: I-JEPA, V-JEPA, and others. But the company, quite understandably, has been putting enormous resources into LLMs and products built on them, because that's where the near-term competition is. That's a legitimate strategic choice. But it means the long-term, somewhat contrarian research doesn't get to be the main thing. And I think this is going to be the next big revolution in AI, in the next few years, not decades. Someone has to go all in on it.

So AMI, Advanced Machine Intelligence, is about doing exactly that: a focused effort on world models, planning, and reasoning, with applications that need real understanding of the physical world: robotics, industrial systems, assistants that can actually help you in the real world, smart glasses, and so on. And I want it to stay open. Open research, open publication. I've always believed progress in AI comes from the whole community, not from one lab locked in a room thinking it has the secret sauce.

And frankly, at my age, I'd like to see this vision realized. Starting something new, built around it, felt like the best way to make that happen.

r001.rationale: He says the long-term world-model research could not be the main focus at Meta, which was prioritizing LLMs, and that pursuing it required a structure built around it. This communicates his judgment that Meta was not the right place to pursue that work.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I should start by saying it wasn't really a sudden decision, and it wasn't a rejection of Meta. I spent twelve years there. I built FAIR, and I'm very proud of what it became. But the thing I've been obsessed with for the last several years, this idea of world models, of AI systems that learn how the world works by observing it, the way a baby or a kitten does, is a long-horizon research program. It's not a product roadmap. And the reality of a large company, particularly in the current climate, is that everything gets pulled toward what can ship in the next few quarters. That's not a criticism. It's just the gravity of the situation.

And I've been saying for a long time that I think the industry is over-indexed on large language models. LLMs are useful, obviously, I'm not saying they're useless. But they are trained on text, and text is a very impoverished representation of reality. A four-year-old has seen more data through their visual system than the biggest LLM has ever seen in text. The child has learned intuitive physics, object permanence, the fact that if you push something it moves. No LLM really understands that. They can regurgitate sentences about it, but they can't plan, they can't reason about the consequences of actions in the physical world, they don't have persistent memory in any meaningful sense. So you cannot get to human-level intelligence, or even cat-level intelligence, by scaling that approach. I'm fairly confident about that.

So the question became, where can I actually do this? I needed a place where the north star is explicitly that: systems that learn world models from sensory data, mostly video, that can predict, that can plan hierarchically, that have the kind of architecture I've been describing with JEPA, joint embedding predictive architectures, where you predict in representation space instead of trying to predict every pixel. Doing that properly requires a team that's committed to it for years, not a group that has to justify itself every planning cycle against the next chatbot feature. AMI Labs, Advanced Machine Intelligence, is that. It's small, it's focused, and the goal is not to compete with the frontier labs on language models. That race is already crowded and frankly I think it's heading toward diminishing returns.

I'd also say, and this is more personal, I'm at a point in my career where I'd rather spend my remaining years on the problem I actually believe will matter, instead of being the guy in the corner saying "this won't work" while everyone else runs in the other direction. Better to go build the alternative and let the results speak. If I'm wrong, we'll find out. But I don't think I'm wrong.

r001.rationale: He says Meta’s focus is pulled toward products that can ship soon, while his world-model research needs years of commitment, and that AMI Labs is the place for that work.

astra-6.text:
The motivation is that I think there is a missing piece in AI: understanding how the world works. Language is part of that, of course, but a system that can give you a fluent answer doesn’t necessarily know what will happen if it takes an action in the physical world.

Think about a household robot. It needs to understand its surroundings, anticipate the consequences of moving an object, and plan a sequence of actions. It has to learn much of that from observation and experience, without someone writing down every rule. That requires what I call a world model—an internal model that lets the system predict consequences before it acts.

That’s the direction I want to pursue with AMI Labs. The attraction of a dedicated organization is being able to make that research agenda the central mission, bringing together the people and resources to turn those ideas into systems that work. It’s a long-term research problem, but I think it is essential if we want AI that can help us beyond the screen.

r001.rationale: The response says AMI Labs can make this research agenda its central mission, but does not state that LeCun left Meta because he judged Meta was not the right place to pursue it.

sol-6.1.text:
The motivation is to pursue a broader vision of intelligence. Language is an important part of it, but an intelligent system also needs to understand how the world works: what happens when you take an action, what you can predict, and what you don’t know. It needs to be able to plan.

I don’t think we get there simply by making language models bigger. We need systems that learn from observing the world and interacting with it, that build internal models they can use to reason about possible outcomes. That’s the research direction I want to focus on. The attraction of starting a lab is the opportunity to organize the whole effort around that long-term objective.

r001.rationale: The response explains the broader research goal and why starting a lab is attractive, but it does not say Meta was not the right place to pursue that goal.
